diseases.description: A fungal disease caused by Puccinia triticina, resulting in small orange-brown pustules on leaves, reducing grain yield.
symptoms: Small, round orange-brown pustules on leaf blades.
Pustules rub off on fingers, leaving a dusty rust-colored residue.
Premature leaf drying and shriveling.
causes: Mild temperatures (15-22°C) combined with high moisture or dew.
prevention: Cultivate rust-resistant wheat cultivars.
Adjust sowing dates to avoid peak rust periods.
Manage nitrogen fertilization to avoid excessive vegetative growth.
bestPractices: Destroy volunteer green plants that serve as host bridges.
Perform field monitoring during the boot and heading stages.

diseases.description: A seed-borne fungal disease caused by Ustilago nuda, where healthy grain heads are replaced by black spore masses.
symptoms: Heads emerge from boot covered in black, dusty spore masses.
Grains are completely replaced by fungal spores.
Spores are blown away by wind, leaving only the bare central stalk.
causes: Infection of flowers in the previous season.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds.
Treat seeds with systemic fungicides before sowing.
Grow resistant wheat varieties.
bestPractices: Perform hot-water seed treatment for organic farming.
Sanitize sowing equipment between fields.

diseases.description: A devastating fungal disease caused by Magnaporthe oryzae, affecting leaves, nodes, and panicles.
symptoms: Spindle-shaped lesions on leaves with gray centers and brown borders.
Rotting of nodes, causing stems to break.
Neck rot, where the base of the panicle rots, causing grains to shrivel.
causes: High relative humidity (over 85-90%) and cool night temperatures.
prevention: Plant blast-resistant rice cultivars.
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization; apply in split doses.
Maintain appropriate water depth in fields.
bestPractices: Avoid overhead irrigation.
Destroy infected straw and stubble after harvest.

diseases.description: A highly destructive bacterial disease caused by Xanthomonas oryzae, causing wilting of seedlings and leaf yellowing.
symptoms: Water-soaked stripes on leaf blades that turn yellow or white.
Wavy margin lesions starting from leaf tips and moving down.
Bacterial droplets (ooze) on leaves in high humidity.
causes: Warm temperatures, high humidity, and rain splash.
Wind and water carrying bacteria between plants.
prevention: Cultivate resistant varieties.
Ensure field drainage to avoid submerging seedlings.
Avoid clipping seedling tips before transplanting.
bestPractices: Keep fields free of weeds that act as bacterial hosts.
Allow fields to dry completely between crop cycles.

diseases.description: A viral disease transmitted by whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci), causing leaf crinkling and stunt growth.
symptoms: Upward or downward curling of leaf margins.
Thickening of leaf veins.
Enation (leaf-like growth) on the underside of leaves.
causes: Presence of weed hosts and alternative host crops.
prevention: Plant CLCuV-resistant cotton varieties.
Implement effective weed management to destroy hosts.
Avoid planting cotton near alternative host plants like okra.
bestPractices: Monitor whitefly populations regularly.
Apply insecticides targeted at whitefly vectors to prevent virus spread.

diseases.description: A bacterial disease caused by Xanthomonas citri, leading to leaf spots, boll rot, and stem blackening.
symptoms: Angular, water-soaked lesions on leaves (angular leaf spot).
Lesions turning brown or black as leaf tissue dies.
Water-soaked spots on bolls that cause lint staining and rot.
causes: Humid conditions and heavy wind-driven rains.
prevention: Use acid-delinted, certified disease-free seed.
Plant resistant cotton varieties.
Incorporate infected crop residue deep into the soil after harvest.
bestPractices: Avoid sprinkler irrigation.
Rotate cotton crops with non-hosts like maize or wheat.

diseases.description: A fungal disease caused by Bipolaris maydis, causing elongated tan lesions on leaves, reducing yield.
symptoms: Elongated, rectangular tan lesions between leaf veins.
Lesions with reddish-brown borders.
Premature leaf drying and death in severe cases.
prevention: Grow resistant maize hybrids.
Rotate maize with legume crops.
Perform deep tillage to bury crop debris.
bestPractices: Ensure balanced nitrogen and potassium fertilization.
Monitor fields starting from the mid-vegetative stage.

diseases.description: A fungal disease caused by Puccinia sorghi, characterized by powdery cinnamon-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces.
symptoms: Oval, golden-brown to cinnamon-brown pustules on leaves.
Pustules rupture to release powdery spores.
Leaves turning yellow and drying under severe infection.
causes: Cool temperatures (16-23°C) and high relative humidity.
Spores carried by wind from southern regions.
prevention: Plant rust-resistant maize varieties.
Use early planting dates to escape late-season spore influx.
Rotate crop sections.
bestPractices: Avoid overhead irrigation in late afternoon.
Remove host plants like wood sorrel.

diseases.description: Fungal infection by Alternaria solani causing target-like leaf spots on tomatoes.
symptoms: Concentric target-board rings on older foliage.
Yellowing surrounding leaf spot margins.
Premature leaf loss starting from bottom foliage.
causes: Warm, humid weather and frequent dew.
Spores overwintering in soil or debris.
prevention: Plant disease-resistant tomato cultivars.
Apply mulch to prevent soil splashing onto foliage.
Rotate crops every 2-3 years.
bestPractices: Prune the lower 12 inches of foliage to prevent soil contact.
Water at base using drip lines to keep leaves dry.

diseases.description: A highly destructive disease caused by Phytophthora infestans, causing rapid leaf wilting and fruit rot.
symptoms: Large, irregular water-soaked lesions on leaves and stems.
Fuzzy white mold on leaf undersides in wet conditions.
Firm, brown leathery lesions on green and ripe tomato fruit.
causes: Wind-blown spores from infected potatoes or tomatoes.
prevention: Plant resistant tomato cultivars.
Destroy volunteer plants and cull piles.
Keep foliage dry and space plants adequately.
bestPractices: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately.
Avoid overhead watering.

diseases.description: A fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani, producing target-like concentric rings on potato leaves.
symptoms: Dark, angular leaf spots with concentric target-like rings.
Leaves turning yellow and falling off prematurely.
Dry, leathery, sunken lesions on potato tubers.
causes: Alternating wet and dry periods on leaf surfaces.
prevention: Maintain crop nutrition (adequate nitrogen and potassium).
Plant certified, disease-free seed tubers.
Practice crop rotation.
bestPractices: Avoid physical injury to tubers during harvest.
Store tubers in cool, dry conditions.

diseases.description: A devastating disease caused by Phytophthora infestans, responsible for the historical Irish Potato Famine.
symptoms: Water-soaked lesions on leaf margins that quickly turn black.
White fungal growth on the underside of leaf lesions.
Rotting of potato tubers, leading to complete crop decay.
causes: High relative humidity (>90%) and mild temperatures (10-24°C).
prevention: Plant certified disease-free potato seeds.
Eliminate volunteer potato plants in surrounding fields.
Monitor disease forecasts during wet weather.
bestPractices: Harvest only when potato vines are dead for at least 14 days.
Store potatoes in ventilated bins with humidity controls.

diseases.description: A common fungal disease caused by Alternaria porri, forming purple lesions on onion leaves and flower stalks.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn brown to purple.
Zonate banding on spots, bordered by a yellow zone.
Bulb decay starting at the neck of the onion.
causes: Warm temperatures (21-30°C) and persistent dew or leaf wetness.
prevention: Use healthy transplants and certified seeds.
Rotate onion crops with non-allium species.
Provide excellent field drainage.
bestPractices: Allow onion necks to dry completely before topping.
Apply balanced nitrogen to prevent weak leaves.

diseases.description: A fungal-like disease caused by Peronospora destructor, producing violet-gray downy mold on onion foliage.
symptoms: Violet-gray downy growth on leaf surfaces during humid mornings.
Pale green or yellow lesions on leaves.
Leaves collapse and die, reducing bulb size.
causes: Spores surviving in soil, wild onions, or set bulbs.
prevention: Avoid planting sets or bulbs showing signs of rot.
Space rows widely to facilitate air movement.
Implement crop rotation of 3-4 years.
bestPractices: Water crops in the morning to allow leaves to dry during the day.
Remove weed hosts that retain field moisture.

diseases.description: A major fungal disease caused by Colletotrichum species, resulting in sunken lesions on chili pods.
symptoms: Sunken, circular lesions on chili fruit (pods).
Concentric rings of orange to black spore masses on pods.
Small, dark, water-soaked leaf spots.
causes: Warm, humid weather, heavy rains, and dew.
Spores splashing from infected debris or soil.
prevention: Use disease-free seed or treat seeds with fungicide.
Remove all crop debris from fields after harvest.
Practice crop rotation.
bestPractices: Avoid overhead irrigation during fruiting.
Harvest fruit regularly and remove rotten pods.

diseases.description: A fungal disease caused by Leveillula taurica, characterized by white powdery growth on leaf undersides.
symptoms: White powdery fungal patches on the underside of leaves.
Yellow spots on the upper leaf surfaces.
Severe leaf dropping, exposing fruit to sunscald.
causes: Warm, dry daytime temperatures combined with humid nights.
prevention: Grow resistant chili cultivars.
Avoid dense planting configurations.
Ensure plants have adequate irrigation and nutrition.
bestPractices: Inspect leaves starting from the lower canopy.
Prune congested center branches to let light penetrate.

diseases.description: A fungal disease caused by Sporisorium scitamineum, producing characteristic black whip-like structures from plant terminals.
symptoms: A black, dusty, whip-like structure emerging from the shoot apex.
Stunted stalks with narrow, erect leaves.
Excessive tillering with thin, grassy shoots.
prevention: Plant smut-resistant sugarcane varieties.
Use hot-water treated seed setts.
Eradicate infected stools at first detection.
bestPractices: Bag infected whips before cutting to prevent spore dispersal.
Rotate sugarcane fields with non-grass crops.

diseases.description: A highly destructive disease caused by Colletotrichum falcatum, causing stalk decay and red internal tissue discoloration.
symptoms: Red discoloration of internal pith with white transverse patches.
Yellowing and drying of leaf canopies, starting from third or fourth leaves.
Hollowing out of stalks, causing a characteristic alcoholic smell.
causes: Planting infected setts or using contaminated water.
prevention: Plant resistant sugarcane cultivars.
Use healthy, disease-free seed setts.
Ensure proper soil drainage and avoid waterlogging.
bestPractices: Uproot and destroy infected clumps.
Apply bio-fungicides or seed treatments prior to planting.
